chunks.text: Long ago, King Aswapati of the Madras had a daughter named Savitri, who set out to find a husband worthy of her and traveled through many sacred places and hermitages before returning home. She found her father seated in his court with the sage Narada, and bowed to them both. Narada asked why Aswapati had not yet given his daughter in marriage, and the king told the sage to hear the answer from Savitri herself.

Savitri told them of a Kshatriya king of the Salwas named Dyumatsena, who had gone blind and was then driven from his kingdom by an old enemy. Dyumatsena withdrew into the forest with his wife and infant son, and took up the life of an ascetic, while the boy grew to manhood in the hermitage. That son, said Savitri, she had chosen in her heart as her husband.

Narada cried out that she had done wrong to choose him, for both his father and his mother were so truthful in speech that the Brahmanas had named the boy Satyavan; as a child he had loved horses, shaping and drawing them, so that he was also called Chitraswa.

Questioned further, Narada said Satyavan was as full of energy as the sun and as wise as Brihaspati, as brave as the lord of the celestials and as forgiving as the earth, as liberal as Rantideva, as truthful and devoted to Brahmanas as Sivi, as magnanimous as Yayati, and as beautiful as the moon.
Asked at last what defect the youth might have, Narada answered that Satyavan had one defect that outweighed all his virtues: within a year of that day, he was destined to die.

Aswapati begged his daughter to choose another husband, but Savitri answered that a woman gives her heart only once, as death comes only once, and a daughter is given away only once; she had chosen Satyavan and would not choose again. Narada declared that her resolve could not be shaken and approved the marriage, then rose into the sky and departed for heaven, while the king began preparing the wedding.

Aswapati traveled with priests to Dyumatsena's forest hermitage and asked the blind king to accept Savitri as his daughter-in-law. Dyumatsena protested that a life of forest hardship was unfit for a princess, but Aswapati insisted he had already made up his mind, and the two kings, once equals, agreed to the match; the wedding rites were performed among the hermits of the forest.

Savitri put aside her ornaments and royal robes for the bark garments of the ascetics, and won the love of her husband and his parents through her service and gentle speech, though Narada's words of the coming year remained in her mind night and day.

When the appointed day at last drew near, Savitri, who had silently counted the days, learned that her husband would die on the fourth day following, and she undertook a fast of three nights and days, the Triratra vow. Dyumatsena, hearing of so hard a vow, grew sorrowful and told her how difficult it would be to fast three nights together, but she said she had the perseverance to complete it, and he told her to go on and finish it.
On the appointed morning, having finished her rites and been blessed by the hermits that she would never become a widow, Savitri told her parents-in-law she would eat only after sunset.

That day Satyavan took up his axe to go into the woods, and Savitri insisted on going with him, saying she could not bear to be parted from him; Satyavan asked her first to seek his parents' leave. Dyumatsena, remembering that Savitri had never before asked anything of him, granted her wish, only asking that Satyavan's errand not be neglected.
Savitri walked beside her husband through the blossoming forest, smiling outwardly though her heart, remembering Narada's words, already grieved for him as one already gone.

Satyavan gathered fruit and began cutting wood, but soon his head began to ache and his whole body with it, and he lay down with his head in Savitri's lap. Then Savitri saw a radiant, red-clad being of terrible aspect, carrying a noose, standing beside her husband and gazing at him; she asked who he was.
He answered that he was Yama, and that Satyavan's allotted days had run out, so he had come himself, rather than send his messengers, because of the young man's rare virtue.

Yama drew out from Satyavan's body a small being bound in his noose, and Satyavan's body at once lay still and lifeless; Yama turned south with his burden, and Savitri, grief-stricken, followed him. Yama told her to turn back, for she had come as far as any living being could, but Savitri answered that she would follow wherever her husband was carried, and spoke to him of virtue and of the good fortune of keeping company with the righteous.
Pleased, Yama offered her a boon — any except her husband's life — and she asked that her blind father-in-law regain his sight and his strength; Yama granted it.

Still Savitri walked on, speaking further words of wisdom, and Yama, delighted, granted a second boon: that Dyumatsena regain his lost kingdom. She asked a third boon: a hundred sons for her own father, Aswapati; it was granted. A fourth boon: a hundred sons for herself, born of Satyavan.

Then Savitri said that this very boon could not be fulfilled without her husband, and asked for a fifth: that Satyavan himself be restored to life, for without him she wished for neither heaven nor prosperity nor happiness.

Yama, saying "so be it," untied his noose and freed Satyavan, promising that he would live four hundred years with Savitri at his side, achieve great fame, and father a hundred sons upon her, and that Aswapati too would have a hundred sons; then Yama departed for his own abode.
Savitri returned to where her husband's body lay, placed his head again on her lap, and he awoke as if from a long sleep, asking where the dark stranger who had been dragging him away had gone.

Meanwhile Dyumatsena had suddenly regained his sight and, with his wife Saivya, had searched the forest all night for their missing son, comforted at last by hermits who assured them, from the signs they read, that Satyavan still lived.

When Savitri and Satyavan returned to the hermitage that night, the sages asked what had delayed them, and Savitri told the whole story: how Narada had foretold the day, how Yama had come and been followed and persuaded, and how five boons had been won — her father-in-law's sight and kingdom, a hundred sons for her father, a hundred sons for herself, and her husband's restored life of four hundred years.
The assembled sages praised her, for by her virtue she had rescued the whole line of the king from its misfortune, and then took their leave.

The next morning, messengers arrived from the kingdom of the Salwas with news that the usurper who had driven out Dyumatsena had himself been slain by his own minister, and that the people wished their rightful king restored, sight or no sight.

Dyumatsena returned to his city and was installed on the throne, with Satyavan made prince-regent beside him; in time Savitri bore a hundred sons, brave in battle, and her father Aswapati likewise had a hundred sons by his queen Malavi. Thus, through her devotion and her wisdom, Savitri raised her husband, his parents, and her own father's house from misfortune to lasting good fortune.
